behavior_items: The reproducer defines two independent primary class templates, Base1<T> and Base2<T>, both of which are empty and have no user-declared constructors. Each therefore has an implicit default constructor.

It then defines a class template Derived<T = int> that multiply inherits from Base1<T> and Base2<T>. The template parameter T has a default argument, so writing Derived without explicit template arguments is intended to allow deduction or fallback to T = int.

Inside Derived, the declarations using Base1<T>::Base1; and using Base2<T>::Base2; request constructor inheritance from both direct base classes. Even though the bases are empty and have no explicit constructors, these using-declarations still participate in the set of constructors considered for the derived class and, importantly, affect the generation of deduction guides for class template argument deduction (CTAD).

The declaration Derived d; is a variable definition that uses the template name without angle brackets, so it triggers CTAD. Because there are no initializer arguments, the compiler must determine whether Derived() can be formed and what template arguments it implies.

Since Derived has a default template argument T = int, one valid conceptual outcome is a deduced type Derived<int>. In normal operation, CTAD should not report ambiguity here: the empty declaration with no constructor arguments should resolve to the defaulted template parameter and produce a default-constructed Derived<int>.

The bug report shows that GCC 14/15 in -std=c++23 instead synthesizes multiple candidate deduction guides or constructor-originated CTAD candidates for the zero-argument case. One candidate is attributed to the inherited constructor machinery associated with Base1, and another candidate is the ordinary candidate associated with Derived itself.

The diagnostic proves this by listing two candidates for the call Derived(): one noted at the Base1 definition site and one at the Derived definition site, both producing the same target type Derived<T> with T = int. GCC then incorrectly treats these equivalent candidates as an ambiguous overload set.

The reproducer therefore exercises the interaction between three language features at once: multiple inheritance, inherited constructors via using-declarations, and class template argument deduction with a default template parameter and no explicit initializer arguments.

The fact that Base2 is also inherited is significant even though the shown diagnostic mentions Base1 and Derived only. The reproducer is specifically stressing that constructor inheritance from multiple bases must not lead to duplicated or competing deduction candidates for the same no-argument construction path.

The bug report notes that the same code succeeds under -std=c++20 and also works on the GCC 13 branch even with -std=c++23. That makes this a regression in newer GCC versions tied to C++23 handling, likely in the compiler logic that forms or ranks CTAD candidates when inherited constructors are present in a multiply inherited class template.

Semantically, there is no real user-visible ambiguity in the source program: both base subobjects are default-constructible, Derived itself is default-constructible, and the default template argument supplies T = int. The ambiguous overload is therefore compiler-internal and indicates that GCC is overcounting equivalent CTAD candidates instead of collapsing or ignoring the inherited-constructor-derived duplicates.

In short, the reproducer is minimal but targeted: empty base templates avoid unrelated constructor complexity, the derived template has only a defaulted parameter, and the naked declaration Derived d; isolates the compiler path where CTAD candidate generation and overload resolution for inherited constructors go wrong.
test_behavior_analysis.summary: This reproducer tests GCC's CTAD handling for a multiply inherited class template that inherits constructors from two base class templates and has a default template argument. The program should allow Derived d; to mean default construction of Derived<int>. Instead, GCC 14/15 in C++23 mode generates multiple zero-argument deduction candidates—apparently one from inherited-constructor processing and one from the class itself—and wrongly reports them as ambiguous. The code therefore exposes a C++23 regression in candidate generation/ranking for CTAD with inherited constructors under multiple inheritance.

test_failure_analysis.analysis: The failure pattern is a front-end semantic regression in GCC's C++23 class template argument deduction (CTAD) path, specifically when a class template with a default template argument multiply inherits from bases and inherits constructors from them via using-declarations. The source is semantically simple: both bases are empty, implicitly default-constructible, and the derived template should be default-constructible as Derived<int> because T has a default argument. The reported ambiguity therefore does not come from the program's meaning but from GCC producing multiple equivalent zero-argument CTAD candidates and then failing to merge, discard, or rank them correctly. The regression boundary is also informative: it works in C++20 and on the GCC 13 branch even in C++23 mode, so a newer C++23-specific change likely altered candidate synthesis or overload resolution for inherited constructors. The common pattern is duplicated deduction-guide or constructor-derived candidate creation for default construction in the presence of inherited constructors from multiple bases, combined with incorrect ambiguity handling for candidates that deduce the same specialization.

For example, given: template <class T> struct S { template <class U> void f(U); }; if TMPL is `template <class U> void S<int>::f(U)' this will return the full template. This function will not trace past partial specializations, however. For example, given in addition: template <class T> struct S<T*> { template <class U> void f(U); }; if TMPL is `template <class U> void S<int*>::f(U)' this will return `template <class T> template <class U> S<T*>::f(U)'.
